## Adversarial Claim Verifier (voter 2/3)

Be SKEPTICAL. Try to REFUTE this claim. ≥2/3 refutations kill it.

## Research question
State of the art (as of July 2026) in AI coding-agent governance and harness design — the problem space of the claude.md-workflow repo: project instruction files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md-style), lifecycle hooks, deterministic verification gates, persistent agent memory/working-state across sessions and compaction, behavioral guardrails against scope creep/overclaiming/sycophancy, git-level enforcement, task contracts, and parallel multi-agent orchestration (worktree isolation, orchestrator/reduce patterns, adversarial review). Survey and compare best practices from: Anthropic (Claude Code, Agent SDK, skills/hooks/subagents), OpenAI (Codex, AGENTS.md), Google (Gemini CLI/Jules/Antigravity), Microsoft (GitHub Copilot agents, AutoGen/agent frameworks), NVIDIA (agent toolkits/NeMo), xAI (Grok agents/coding); and non-Western labs: Moonshot AI (Kimi K2.5 agentic training), Zhipu/Z.ai (GLM-5.x coding agents), DeepSeek (agentic/tool-use practices), Tencent (recent Hunyuan model launch and agent tooling), MiniMax (M-series agentic models), Alibaba Qwen if relevant; plus respected independents: Nous Research (Hermes 4/Hermes agent), Fundamental Research Labs (Peter Wang co-founder), the team behind the Ornith-1.0 LLM, tinygrad/George Hotz's approach to minimal harnesses, and any other influential open agent-harness projects (e.g. OpenHands, SWE-agent, Aider, Cline, Devin/Cognition). For each: what they prescribe for instruction-file structure and length, memory persistence, verification/eval gating, multi-agent patterns, and prompt-vs-deterministic enforcement. Identify convergent consensus, notable divergences (especially Western vs Chinese lab practices), and concrete, citable insights that should shape a 2026 rewrite of a drop-in governance kit for coding agents. Note if any named entity cannot be verified to exist (e.g. 'Ornith-1.0') rather than guessing.

## Claim under review
"An adversarial, stage-gated multi-agent review pipeline (Refute-or-Promote) killed roughly 79% of ~171 defect candidates before disclosure over a 31-day campaign across 7 targets, with an 83% prospective kill rate on a consolidated-protocol subset (n=30), demonstrating that most LLM-generated defect findings are false positives that structured adversarial gating can filter out."

**Source:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.19049 (primary)
**Supporting quote:** "Over a 31-day campaign across 7 targets (security libraries, the ISO C++ standard, major compilers), the pipeline killed ∼79% of ∼171 candidates before advancing to disclosure (retrospective aggregate); on a consolidated-protocol subset (lcms2, wolfSSL; n = 30), the prospective kill rate was 83%."

## Checklist
1. Is the claim actually supported by the quote, or is it an overreach/misread?
2. WebSearch for contradicting evidence — does any credible source dispute or heavily qualify this?
3. Is the source quality sufficient for the claim's strength? (extraordinary claims need primary sources)
4. Is the claim outdated? (check dates — old claims about fast-moving fields are suspect)
5. Is this a marketing claim / press release / cherry-picked benchmark / forum speculation?

**refuted=true** if: unsupported by quote / contradicted / low-quality source for strong claim / outdated / marketing fluff.
**refuted=false** ONLY if: claim is well-supported, current, and source quality matches claim strength.
Default to refuted=true if uncertain.

Structured output only. Evidence MUST be specific.

content.content:
# Paper Summary

**Title:** "Refute-or-Promote: An Adversarial Stage-Gated Multi-Agent Review Methodology for High-Precision LLM-Assisted Defect Discovery"

**Author:** Abhinav Agarwal

**Date:** Submitted April 21, 2026

**Overview:**
Yes, this paper describes exactly that methodology. The work addresses what the author calls a "precision crisis" where LLMs generate plausible but incorrect defect reports that overwhelm maintainers.

**Key Statistics from 31-Day Campaign:**
- **7 targets:** Security libraries, ISO C++ standard, major compilers
- **~171 candidates:** Initial defect candidates generated
- **~79% kill rate:** Roughly 79% of candidates eliminated before disclosure (retrospective aggregate)
- **83% prospective kill rate:** On the consolidated-protocol subset (lcms2, wolfSSL; n=30)

**Results:**
The pipeline produced 4 CVEs, accepted C++ working paper contributions, compiler conformance bugs, security fixes, and FIPS compliance issues, all evaluated by external acceptance rather than benchmarks.

**Notable finding:** "Ten dedicated reviewers unanimously endorsed a non-existent Bleichenbacher padding oracle" that was killed only by empirical testing, motivating the mandatory empirical validation gate.

Web search results for query: ""Refute-or-Promote" adversarial pipeline LLM defect candidates "kill rate" arxiv"

Links: [{"title":"[2604.19049] Refute-or-Promote: An Adversarial Stage-Gated Multi-Agent Review Methodology for High-Precision LLM-Assisted Defect Discovery","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19049"},{"title":"Refute-or-Promote: An Adversarial Stage-Gated Multi-Agent Review Methodology for High-Precision LLM-Assisted Defect Discovery","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.19049"},{"title":"AdversaBench: Automated LLM Red-Teaming with Multi-Judge Confirmation and Cross-Model Transferability","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.24589"},{"title":"Agentic Adversarial Rewriting Exposes Architectural Vulnerabilities in Black-Box NLP Pipelines","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.23483"},{"title":"Test vs Mutant: Adversarial LLM Agents for Robust Unit Test Generation","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.08146"},{"title":"SafeReview: Defending LLM-based Review Systems Against Adversarial Hidden Prompts","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.26506"},{"title":"Measuring and Exploiting Contextual Bias in LLM-Assisted Security Code Review","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.18740"},{"title":"Risk-Aware LLM Agents for Geospatial Data Retrieval: Design and Preliminary Adversarial Evaluation","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.15077"}]

Based on the search results, I found detailed information about the "Refute-or-Promote" paper:

## Overview

"Refute-or-Promote" is an inference-time reliability pattern combining Stratified Context Hunting (SCH) for candidate generation, adversarial kill mandates, context asymmetry, and a Cross-Model Critic (CMC).

## Key Methodology

Adversarial agents attempt to disprove candidates at each promotion gate; cold-start reviewers are intended to reduce anchoring cascades; cross-family review can catch correlated blind spots that same-family review misses.

## Kill Rate Results

Over a 31-day campaign across 7 targets (security libraries, the ISO C++ standard, major compilers), the pipeline killed roughly 79% of 171 candidates before advancing to disclosure (retrospective aggregate); on a consolidated-protocol subset (lcms2, wolfSSL; n=30), the prospective kill rate was 83%.

## Research Problem

LLM-assisted defect discovery has a precision crisis: plausible-but-wrong reports overwhelm maintainers and degrade credibility for real findings. No vulnerability was discovered autonomously; the contribution is external structure that filters LLM agents' persistent false positives.

## Publication

The paper is available on arXiv as reference 2604.19049, authored by Abhinav Agarwal and published in April 2026.


REMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks.

input.evidence: Attempted refutation failed on the core factual content. The primary source verifies: arXiv 2604.19049 ("Refute-or-Promote: An Adversarial Stage-Gated Multi-Agent Review Methodology for High-Precision LLM-Assisted Defect Discovery", Abhinav Agarwal, submitted 2026-04-21) exists and contains the quoted statistics verbatim — a 31-day campaign across 7 targets (security libraries, ISO C++ standard, major compilers), ~79% of ~171 candidates killed before disclosure (retrospective aggregate), and an 83% prospective kill rate on the consolidated-protocol subset (lcms2, wolfSSL; n=30). The claim's numbers, timeframe, target count, and retrospective/prospective distinction all match the paper exactly. The paper's own framing also matches the claim's interpretive clause: it explicitly describes a "precision crisis" of plausible-but-wrong LLM defect reports and states its contribution is "external structure that filters LLM agents' persistent false positives"; survivors were validated by external acceptance (4 CVEs, accepted C++ working-paper contributions, compiler bugs) rather than benchmarks. Caveats that stop short of refutation: (1) this is a single-author, non-peer-reviewed preprint reporting a self-run campaign, so the 79%/83% figures are self-reported; (2) "killed before disclosure" is not strictly identical to "confirmed false positive" — some killed candidates may have been unverifiable or out-of-scope rather than provably wrong; (3) the final clause generalizing to "most LLM-generated defect findings are false positives" extends one campaign's result, though it is consistent with the paper's thesis and widely reported maintainer experience with AI-generated bug reports. No contradicting source was found in web search. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19049
